record.text:
Scaled dot‑product attention takes each query vector, computes its dot product with every key vector to measure similarity, divides those scores by √d_k, passes them through a softmax to get a set of weights, and then forms a weighted sum of the corresponding value vectors using those weights [S1][S4].  
Dividing by √d_k prevents the dot products from becoming too large when the dimensionality d_k is high; without this scaling the softmax would enter regions with very small gradients, hurting learning [S2].

record.text: Multiple attention heads allow the model to attend to different representation sub‑spaces simultaneously, so each head can focus on distinct linguistic patterns such as anaphora resolution or long‑distance dependencies rather than a single head trying to capture all relations at once【S2】. By running several attention layers in parallel the Transformer can learn diverse tasks within the same layer, which improves its expressive power【S1】. The paper therefore adopts eight parallel attention heads (h = 8), each with dimensionalities d_k = d_v = d_model / h = 64, keeping the overall computational cost comparable to a single full‑dimensional attention head【S3】.

record.text: The Transformer adds a positional encoding vector of the same dimension \(d_{model}\) to each token embedding, where each entry of the encoding is defined by a sinusoid that depends on the token’s position \(pos\) and the dimension index \(i\) [S1]. Specifically, for even dimensions the value is \(\sin(pos/10000^{2i/d_{model}})\) and for odd dimensions it is \(\cos(pos/10000^{2i/d_{model}})\), giving a set of sinusoids with wavelengths that form a geometric progression from \(2\pi\) to \(10000·2\pi\) [S4]. The authors also tried learned positional embeddings, but found performance essentially identical to the sinusoidal version [S3]. They preferred the sinusoidal encodings because the fixed functions make it easy for the model to represent relative positions as linear combinations and because they may enable the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than seen during training [S3][S4].

Finally, the maximum path length between any two positions is \(O(1)\) for self‑attention but \(O(n)\) for recurrent layers [S2].

record.text: Traditional spoken dialogue systems are built as pipelines of separate components—voice activity detection, speech recognition, textual dialogue processing, and text‑to‑speech—rather than as an integrated model. This modular architecture introduces several seconds of latency between user utterances and system responses, disrupting the flow of conversation. Moreover, because text serves as the intermediate representation, important non‑linguistic cues such as emotion or non‑speech sounds are discarded, preventing the system from capturing the full meaning of an interaction. These factors together prevent conventional systems from emulating the seamless, natural experience of real‑world conversations [S2].

record.text: Moshi is built around three key parts: (1) modules that process the incoming audio streams from both Moshi and the user, (2) modules that handle Moshi’s own text‑token streams, and (3) a Depth Transformer that jointly models these audio and text streams and supports streaming inference [S1].

record.text:
Moshi is built as a multi‑stream speech‑to‑speech Transformer that generates two parallel streams of semantic and acoustic tokens—one for the user and one for the system—so it can listen and speak at the same time [S4][S3].  
By hierarchically streaming these token streams and aligning them with time‑aligned text tokens, Moshi maintains a continuous flow of information from both sides without a fixed turn‑taking boundary [S3].  
This dual‑stream architecture lets Moshi “always listen and can speak at any moment,” achieving true full‑duplex interaction [S1].  
Because each side’s speech is represented separately, the model can process overlapping utterances jointly rather than collapsing them into a single stream [S3].  
The separation of user and system token streams, combined with the underlying Helium text language model, enables Moshi to reason and generate speech in real time even when both participants talk simultaneously [S3].

record.text: Inner Monologue is a modeling approach that treats speech and text as interchangeable token streams, allowing the same foundation model to be used for different modalities by simply adjusting the temporal relationship between those token types [S1][S2]. By inserting a fixed delay between text and audio tokens, the model can be repurposed as a streaming system: delaying audio tokens by a few seconds gives the model look‑ahead on the text, enabling streaming text‑to‑speech when the text tokens are teacher‑forced at inference [S3]. Conversely, delaying text tokens by a similar amount lets the model listen to incoming audio before emitting text, yielding a streaming automatic‑speech‑recognition system when the audio tokens are teacher‑forced at inference [S3]. This simple delay‑based reconfiguration lets Moshi derive both streaming TTS and streaming ASR without changing the underlying architecture [S2].
